item.title: Hiding Grades at College Isn't the Answer
item.description:
Education

Hiding Grades at College Isn't the Answer

10 reasons why concealing grades sets a bad precedent.

Posted August 14, 2026

It was announced last week that starting in 2027, the University of Michigan’s College of Literature, Science, and the Arts will do away with letter grades for first-semester students. As a professor for over 30 years and the author of The Complete U: Over 100 Lessons for Success in and out of the College Classroom, I read this with great interest and even graver concern.

Source: Mikheil Kuzmidi/ Unsplash

As a faculty member who has long been concerned with student well-being, I resent the way that, in this schema, the actions of faculty are held responsible for students’ mental health. When students elect to attend college, it may be for the whole of the experience, yet arguably a centerpiece of it is mastery of coursework. It’s baffling to remove the evaluative aspect of that endeavor before students even arrive, all in the name of mental health.

For years, I’ve wished we could do away with grades, so you might think I’d embrace this. But I’ve been watching over the years how some instructors across the country have been embracing trends du jour like ungrading, specifications grading, and anti-racist grading to name a few. A basic problem with all of these is that professors can decide within the context of their own classes to eliminate grades, but it doesn’t take away the fact that we all must submit them to the registrar at the end of the semester. And these strategies also oddly fetishize grades while aiming not to. This is all to say that there have been movements on the ground to try to change the grading system.

But this kind of change at Michigan, and some other colleges as well, seems to carry with it a different host of problems that I identify here:

  1. The first semester is arguably an important time for students to see where they stand after coming from high schools where grade inflation is fully out of control, especially now with both the weighted GPA and the unweighted GPA and some people having well over a 5.0. High school grades feel obviously false given the ways students are coming to college ill-prepared on so many levels.
  2. Concealing grades is an exercise in denial which is antithetical to showing students how to manage mental health issues. This might be the greatest travesty of all: institutional collusion in not tackling mental health issues head on and honestly.
  3. Asking professors to submit actual grades that then get converted to pass/fail grades render invisible the work of faculty (grading is seriously the worst part of teaching, along with navigating misguided administrative decisions). The news stories indicate that grades would still be recorded for purposes of scholarships and such. Students who eventually find out how they did, especially if they barely passed or did not do as well as they wanted, are surely still going to complain.
  4. At a time in history in which higher education and expertise are undermined in the political arena, colleges and universities should not participate in exacerbating that.
  5. This raises questions about the sort of coursework a student might be taking in the first semester such that mastery would not matter. When I think of fields like healthcare and engineering, for example, it seems we want people to master concepts in biology, anatomy, and chemistry, especially as we consider aging, health and illness, or food sanitation methods and bridge building.
  6. This strategy seems to prolong the inevitable, which is that at a certain point students are going to know what their grades are, and they’re going to have to manage the reality of that along with the rest of their life at college.
  7. Students need practice early on when they’re not doing well to seek out resources at school and to be able to talk with faculty directly, and this strategy instead advocates for “Go have fun and get settled, and we’ll worry about work and grades later.”
  8. Grades can serve as an important barometer that assist faculty in early intervention with struggling students, reaching out to them with care and concern. These conversations need to happen without any sugarcoating. When I reflect on the thousands of hours I’ve spent listening to students, I’m reminded that grades are typically the smallest part of their despair and fear. Instead, I hear about the anguish and stress of family dynamics, grief and death, dating violence and sexual assault, the impact of social media, and fears about the brokenness of the world.
  9. Importantly, this model seems to be a setup for schools grabbing money because if a student is barely passing after the first semester, they’ll very likely stay for the next semester, but if grades were revealed immediately, that same student may not return (an obscene money grab when people’s livelihoods and loan problems are on the line).
  10. Neither the origin nor the solution to the problem of students’ mental health is grades. College is the time for students to learn for themselves how to recover from failure, disappointments, and other missteps; it’s the best place to try, to fail, and to recover.

item.title: 10 Things Estranged Adults Are Told They're Doing Wrong
item.description:
Boundaries

10 Things Estranged Adults Are Told They're Doing Wrong

The compassion extended to grieving parents is needed for adult children as well.

Posted August 14, 2026

Key points
  • Estrangement is usually the end of years of failed repair, not an impulsive decision.
  • The messages estranged adult children hear are often formed without knowing the full story.
  • Compassion for estranged parents and adult children can coexist without taking sides.

A recent post made a thoughtful case on behalf of estranged parents. It argued that ordinary human responses, like explaining, asking questions, or reaching out, are too readily reframed as manipulation, making parents become frightened of their own instincts. There is truth in this, and it needed saying.

Adult children carry a version of this too.

Family, friends, and even people who barely know the situation often form an opinion in seconds, without knowing what actually happened, and that opinion becomes something the adult child now has to carry.

This isn't about deciding who's right. It's about naming the messages that get handed to estranged adult children before anyone has heard their story, and asking whether those messages hold up once you look at them closely.

1. Cutting Off Instead of Working It Out

The message: "You didn't even try. Families talk things through."

What's probably true instead: In both the research and my work with clients, estrangement is rarely a first resort. More typically, it's the final chapter of a much longer story: years of raised concerns, boundaries that did not hold, and hope renewed but disappointed (Agllias, 2016; Scharp, 2019). Others see the decision; they rarely see the years of trying that preceded it.

2. Being Too Sensitive

The message: "Every generation had it tough. You're making a wound out of an upbringing."

What they often miss: Naming harm is not fragility. The person who was hurt carries the moment vividly; the person who caused it may barely remember it at all. This asymmetry belongs to how memory works, not to oversensitivity. Responding to a pattern that ran through childhood is not weakness. It is recognition.

3. Being Ungrateful

The message: "After everything they did for you..."

The missing context: Being provided for isn't the same as feeling emotionally safe. Appreciating what a parent gave you doesn't override what caused you harm emotionally. Most estranged adult children can name exactly what their parents gave them, no problem. That's part of what makes the loss so confusing. You're not ungrateful. You're actually grieving something with two sides.

article continues after advertisement

4. Airing Family Business

The message: "What happens in this family stays in this family."

What gets left out: When someone cannot speak openly about what is happening, harmful patterns are more likely to carry on. Speaking to trusted people, such as a friend, a therapist, or a support group, is how human beings process loss and difficult experiences. Pressure for secrecy tends to protect the system rather than the people within it.

5. Overreacting to One Incident

The message: "All of this over one comment at Christmas?"

What people don't see: The incident other people can see is often not the whole story behind why someone is taking distance. It's often just the tipping point at which the accumulated weight of detrimental patterns of behavior (which others don't see) became impossible to ignore. One side remembers an event. The other, however, remembers a pattern stretching across many years. That's why one apology, one conversation, or one promise to move on often isn't enough to resolve it.

6. Punishing Their Parents

The message: "This is cruelty. You're using silence as a weapon."

The likelier explanation: From the outside, self-protection and punishment look identical; only their function differs. The adult children I have sat with rarely describe an attack; they describe the moment they stopped hoping the relationship could safely continue, something closer to surrender. What reads as malice is, more often, exhaustion.

7. Being Brainwashed by Therapy or the Internet

The message: "Your therapist put this idea in your head."

What it overlooks: This turns an adult’s considered decision into somebody else’s idea, the very thing parents object to when their grief is dismissed as pathology. In my experience, people come to therapy because of distress that's already there. It's not the other way around. And yes, online spaces can cement narratives on every side. But that doesn't mean a considered adult decision was planted there by a stranger on the internet.

8. Not Accepting the Apology

The message: "They said sorry. What more do you want?"

A different way to see it: The same rules apply here as they would with anyone else. "I'm sorry you feel that way" isn't really an apology. It's a way of ending the conversation without naming what the apology is for. A real apology says what happened and backs it up with change over time, not just the words. Somehow, when it's a parent, people expect those rules to bend. Family is assumed to be the one relationship where you accept less and call it love. It isn't.

article continues after advertisement

9. Refusing to Forgive

The message: "It's your mom [or dad]. You should just forgive them."

What's actually going on: Forgiveness demanded on someone's schedule isn't forgiveness; it's compliance. That doesn't change no matter whose name is on the other end of it. And, like an apology, forgiving someone doesn't settle the question of contact on its own. You can believe them, forgive completely, and still not be ready to let them back in. You can release the resentment and, with sadness, still know the relationship isn't safe to resume. Those are two different things.

10. Wanting Conditions for Reconnection

The message: "Real family doesn't come with terms and conditions."

The gap: Asking for changed behavior before resuming contact is what boundaries look like in every other adult relationship. Yet we seem to find it unreasonable between a parent and adult child. And when the boundary itself is treated as the problem, that often demonstrates exactly why the distance became necessary in the first place.

Why These Narratives Undermine Repair

When every act of self-protection is recast as a moral failure, adult children are reminded that there's no way back that doesn't cost them the truth of their own realities.

Most people will not walk back through a door that requires them to leave parts of themselves outside it. This paradox mirrors the one that parents face: The same condemnation intended to push people back toward family is what makes repair less likely, not more.

For the People Around Them

If someone you love is estranged from a parent, offer compassion and patience. Trust that the decision was harder than it looked from where you are standing. Ask whether they want your thoughts or simply for you to be alongside them. And resist the familiar lines: that they're still your parent, that you'll regret this one day. Both feel like pressure rather than wisdom.

article continues after advertisement

If you are a therapist, neither push reconciliation nor cheer estrangement. Our work is our client's clarity, not the outcome.

In Closing

I don't see this as a choice between defending parents or defending adult children. Parents can grieve deeply, and adult children can still need space and distance. Both can be true at once.

Parents deserve space to grieve without being presumed guilty. Adult children deserve the space to protect themselves without being presumed cruel. Compassion in both directions is not what I would see as sitting on the fence. I believe it is the starting point for understanding what has actually happened and, where possible, for creating the conditions for repair.

item.title: Maybe Thinking You Could Leave Is a Good Sign
item.description:
Relationships

Maybe Thinking You Could Leave Is a Good Sign

New evidence indicates barriers to leaving a relationship are a risk factor.

Posted August 14, 2026

Key points
  • Perceiving barriers to leaving a relationship has been conceptualized as a sign of commitment.
  • Recent evidence suggests that barriers to leaving predict depression, anxiety, and drug use.
  • For some, perceiving barriers to leaving a relationship may indicate they feel trapped or hopeless.
  • Sexual and gender minority people may express commitment in other ways.

Established relationship theory suggests that perceiving barriers to leaving a relationship is a sign of commitment. It is a psychological relationship maintenance strategy – an asset – that increases personal motivation to maintain a relationship (Rusbult, 1980, 1983).

In some ways, this is a logical conclusion. Imagine a person who has been in his relationship for 10 years, he lives with his partner, they share financial costs, and they have a strong social network of friends and family who know them as a couple. Now imagine that in a moment of frustration, this person thinks about leaving his partner. Doing so would require disentangling 10 years of living together. They would need to change their living situation, find a way to meet financial obligations, and also explain the breakup to their family and friends.

These barriers to leaving have the potential to motivate the individual to engage with his partner, repair the relationship, and maintain it into the future. Assuming the relationship is otherwise healthy, this could be considered a good thing. In that case, we would expect it to be negatively associated with mental health problems like anxiety, depression, and substance use. See my previous post for more on relationship quality and mental health.

In a recent study in Psychology of Sexual Orientation and Gender Diversity, my colleagues and I present evidence that defies conventional wisdom (Starks et al., 2026, April). The study involved 192 sexual minority men in relationships, recruited through social networking applications. Participants completed a brief online survey. The majority (93%) had a non-monogamous sexual agreement.

Contrary to expectations, we found that perceived barriers to leaving a relationship were positively associated with anxiety and depression. This follows our earlier study of male couples, which found that barriers to leaving a relationship were positively associated with illicit drug use (Starks et al., 2019). In other words, for these (mostly non-monogamous) sexual minority men, perceptions of barriers to leaving a relationship look like a psychosocial risk factor rather than an asset.

Conventional wisdom in relationship science is largely influenced by research on heterosexual people. One possible explanation for these findings is that sexual minority men understand this construct differently than heterosexual people do. Believing that it would be hard to leave a relationship may translate to feeling trapped or hopelessly stuck in a relationship.

It is also possible that sexual minority men have alternative ways of expressing commitment that are not captured by current measures of relationship quality (which were mostly developed in heterosexual samples). This could be particularly true for those with non-monogamous sexual agreements.

Conclusions

article continues after advertisement

Relationship commitment is a sign of high relationship quality; however, it is not clear that perceiving barriers to leaving a relationship is a particularly good indicator of commitment for sexual minority men. In fact, it might be a sign of feeling trapped in or hopeless about a relationship. Future research is needed to understand the strategies sexual and gender minority people use to maintain the long-term durability of their relationships.
